La sirena de una ambulancia suena más ag: An ambulance siren sounds higher when it approaches and lower when it leaves, even though the siren always emits the same. And a radar knows how fast you are going just by listening to the echo of its waves. What do they have in common?

<b>1842</b>Christian Doppler, profesor e: 1842Christian Doppler, a professor in Prague, proposes that the colour of double stars changes depending on whether they approach or recede from us. For stars he was wrong about the size of the effect, but the idea was good.
<b>1845</b>Christophorus Buys Ballot lo: 1845Christophorus Buys Ballot tests it with sound in Utrecht: he puts musicians on a train passing at full speed playing a fixed note, and other musicians on the platform, with a good ear, notice how the pitch changes.
<b>1868</b>William Huggins mide el corri: 1868William Huggins measures the shift of the lines in the spectrum of Sirius and calculates how fast it is moving: the Doppler effect becomes a tool of astronomy.
<b>1947</b>Aparecen los primeros radares: 1947The first speed radars for the police appear in the United States. Today traffic ones work at around 24 GHz or 34 GHz, or with laser.
La sirena es una fuente que se mueve hac: The siren is a source moving towards a stationary observer, and the radar is an echo off a moving obstacle: two Doppler effects in a row, first the car as observer and then as source.

Estás en la acera y se acerca una ambula: You are on the pavement and an ambulance approaches. While it comes, the siren sounds high; just as it passes by you, the pitch drops suddenly and moves away lower. The driver, on the other hand, always hears it the same.\n\nIt is the Doppler effect: the frequency that is heard depends on how the source and the listener move. And it is the same thing a traffic radar uses to know how fast you are going.
Delante, los frentes de onda se amontona: In front, the wavefronts pile up
es lo que oyes mientras la ambulancia se: is what you hear while the ambulance approaches at 90 km/h.
La sirena lanza un frente de onda cada 1: The siren launches a wavefront every 1/700 s, which moves away at 340 m/s in all directions. But the ambulance, at 25 m/s, is chasing its own wavefronts, and those in front come out closer together: $λ_1 = (v − v_F)/f = (340 − 25)/700 = 0.45 "m"$, instead of 0.486 m.\n\nMore wavefronts reach you each second, so you hear a higher pitch: $f_1 = f v/(v − v_F) = 700 · 340/315 = 755.6 "Hz"$.
baja el tono al pasar: dos semitonos y m: the pitch drops as it passes: two and a half semitones.
Detrás de la ambulancia los frentes qued: Behind the ambulance the wavefronts are further apart and fewer arrive per second: $f_2 = f v/(v + v_F) = 700 · 340/365 = 652.1 "Hz"$.\n\nAs it passes, the pitch drops from 755.6 Hz to 652.1 Hz. The faster the source goes, the bigger the jump. In the drawing the ambulance goes much faster than in reality so you can see how the wavefronts pile up.
es la frecuencia de muchos radares de tr: is the frequency of many traffic radars: λ = 1.25 cm.
Un radar de tráfico hace lo mismo con on: A traffic radar does the same with electromagnetic waves, which travel at the speed of light, $c = 3·10^8 "m/s"$. It launches 24 GHz microwaves at the cars and picks up those that bounce off them.\n\nThe wave is invisible and cannot be heard, but the radar can compare with great precision the frequency it sends with the one that comes back.
El eco trae dos efectos Doppler: The echo brings two Doppler effects
más trae el eco de un coche a 33 m/s (un: more is what the echo of a car at 33 m/s brings (about 119 km/h).
El coche recibe la onda como un observad: The car receives the wave as an approaching observer, $f_R = f (c + u)/c$, and returns it as an approaching source, $f″ = f_R c/(c − u)$. The effect is added twice: $f″ ≈ f (1 + 2u/c)$.\n\nFor $u = 33 "m/s"$, $Δf = 2 u f/c = 2 · 33 · 24 "GHz"/(3·10^8) = 5280 "Hz"$: barely two ten-millionths of the frequency. The radar mixes the wave it sends with the echo and measures the beats, which go exactly at Δf.
de diferencia en el eco: se mide sin pro: of difference in the echo: it is measured without a problem.
Despejando la velocidad: $u = c Δf/(2 f): Solving for the speed: $u = c Δf/(2 f) = 3·10^8 · 5280/(2 · 24·10^9) = 33 "m/s"$, that is, 118.8 km/h. If the road is limited to 100, the flash goes off.\n\nThe radar only measures the part of the speed that goes towards it, $u cos α$: that is why it is placed almost in line with the road. Doppler ultrasound measures the speed of blood in the same way, and weather radars, that of the wind with the rain.
